Τ Ε Λ Ο Σ .
english:
THE LIFE OF PLATO.

Of things that exist, some are called according to themselves kath' heauta in themselves, and some are called in relation to something else. Those called according to themselves are as many as need nothing else in their definition. These would be, for example, human, horse, and other animals, for none of these proceeds through definition. Of those called in relation to something else are as many as need some definition, for example, the greater is greater than something, and the faster is faster than something, and the more beautiful is more beautiful than something, and such things. For the greater is greater than the smaller, and the faster is faster than something. Therefore, of things that exist, some are said to be by themselves, and some in relation to something else. Thus he also divided the first principles according to Aristotle.

There was also another philosopher named Plato from Rhodes, a student of Panaetius, as Seleucus the grammarian says in the first book concerning philosophy. And another was a Peripatetic, a student of Aristotle. And another of Praxiphanes, and the poet of the Old Comedy.

THE END.

author: Plato, v427-v347
greek:
Εἶπε Πλάτων ξυνοπαδὲ θεοῖς καὶ δαίμοσιν ἥρως
    Πασσυδίῃ μεγάλῳ Ζηνὶ παρεσπομένοις,
Ἅρμα κατ’ οὐρανὸν εὐρὺ ἀελλοπόδων ὅτε πώλων
    Κάνθῳ ἐλᾷ πτηνῷ δίφρῳ ἐφεζόμενος.
Εἰ δ’ ἄγε νῦν κατάβηθι λιπὼν χορὸν οὐρανιώνων,
    Ἐς γαῖ’ ψυχοφυῶν αἱρεσίν ἡμετέρων.
Καὶ λάιζου τόδε τεῦχος, ὅ Σωκρατικῶν ὀαριστὺν
    Ἀμφὶς ἔχει, καὶ σῆς κλείνὰ γένεθλα φρενός.
ᾦ χὐπὸ κοσμοτέχνης ὀκτὼ πτύχας οὐλύμποιο
    Ἐξ ἰδίων ἕλκων ἀρχέτυπον πραπίδων,
Δείματο καρπαλίμως· ὑπάτω σέλαέσσιν ἀπείροις
    Δαιδάλλων, τὴν πῦρ κλείουσι ἀπλανέα.
Τὰς δ’ ἄρ ὑφεξείης μονοφεγγέας ἐξετόρευσε
    Αὐτόθεν ἀπροστάτης ἀντία κινυμένας.
Ἡ σφέας ἁρπάζουσα παλιμπλάγκτοιο κελεύθου
    Σύρει ἀναγκαίῃ, ταὶ δὲ βιαζόμεναι
Οὐκ ἄκουσαι ἕπονται· ὅμως ἑὸν οἶμον ἑκάστη
    Ἔμπαλιν ἐξανύει βάρδιον ἢ τάχιον.
ᾦ χὐπὸ κυκλεὸς ἔρως ἀπ’ γαίης ὑψόσ’ ἀείρων,
    Ἱμέρῳ ἄμμε φλέγει κάλλεος οὐρανίου.
ᾦ χὐπὸ σὺ ψυχᾶς φύσιν ἄφθορον, οὐ δ’ ἀμυδρωσοῦ
    Σκιώδης ὀλυμπίου δάξας ἀπολλυμένω.
Ἄλλοτε διαγραφῶν πόλιν οὐρανογείτονα φωτῶν
    Κτίζες, οἷσι μέλει πότνια δικαιοσύνη,
Ἡ δὲ καὶ εὐνομίη κουροτρόφος· οὐ δ’ ἀπ’ ἐκείνου
    Νόσφιν ἀπετραπέτην ἄστεος· ὅστε πάλιν
Αἰδὼς καὶ νέμεσις· τίς ἕκαστά κε μυθολογύοι
    Ὅσσα θεοπνεύστοις ταῖς δ’ ἐνέθου σελίσι.
Τάς γε λαβὼν ἀφίκοιο πόλιν βασιλίδ’ ἁπασέων,
    Ὅσσας οὐρανόθεν δέρκεται ἠέλιος,
Ῥώμην ἑπτάλοφον γαίης κράτος αἰὲν ἔχουσαν.
    Ἡς διὰ μεσσατίης Θύμβρις ἑλισσόμενος
Κοίρανος ἑσπερίων ποταμῶν κερατηφόρος εἶσιν
    Οὖθαρ πιαίνων βώλακος Αὐσονίης.
Ἐλθὼν δ’ οὐ σικελῶν ὀλοόφρονα κεῖθι τύραννον
    Ὠμοφάγου σκύλλης λυγαλέης τρόφιμον,
Ὑβριστὴν μουσέων Διονύσιον, ἀλλά γε δῖας
    Ὧ τόδ’ ὁμοῖον ἰδεῖν φῶτα μάτιν ἐπόθεις.
Ἀμφότερον σοφίης τε πρόμον καὶ ποιμένα λαῶν
    Ὁππόσοι Εὐρώπην ναιετάουσιν ὅλην.
Λαυριάδην ἐρατῆς φλωρεντίδος ἀστέρα πάτρης
    Λαμπρόν. ἀτὰρ Μεδίκων τῶν ὀνομαστοτάτων,
Τηλεθόον καλὸν ἔρνος ἀθααλὲς ἀγλαόκαρπον
    Τοπρὶν Ἰωάννην, νῦν δ’ ἄρ’ ἀπειρεσίαν
Γαιάων διέποντα ΛΕΟΝΤΑ, κράτισον ὀλύμπου
    Κληδοῦχον, τῷ νῦν ὡς διὸς ἀζόμεθα.
Πᾶς ὅν ἄναξ σέβεται γονυούμενος, οὐ δέ τις αὐτῷ
    Τολμᾷ σκηπτούχων ἀντιφερίζεμεναι.
Εἰσβὰς δ’ ὀλβιόδαιμον ἀνάκτορον, εὐθὺς ἐραστὰς
    Σᾶο Πλάτων πολλοὺς ὄψεαι ἐν μεγάροις.
Παιδείαις ἀρεταῖσι μεμηλότας· ἠδ’ ὀαριστὰς
    Τερπνοὺς καὶ πινυτοῦ ζωὸς ἐπιχθονίου.
english:
M. MUSURUS.

O Plato, hero and companion to the gods and spirits,
    Who follow in the wake of great Zeus with your whole company,
When you drive your chariot across the wide heavens,
    Seated in a winged carriage, drawn by storm-footed steeds.
But come now, descend, leaving the choir of the heavenly ones,
    To the earth for the choice of our souls.
And take up this volume, which holds the conversation of the Socratics,
    And the glorious progeny of your own mind.
By which, as a master-craftsman, you drew the eight folds of Olympus
    From your own original thoughts,
And fashioned them quickly, decorating them with the highest infinite lights,
    Which they call the fixed fire.
And those that follow, you carved one by one, glowing alone,
    Moving naturally against the uncontrolled ones.
The one  snatching them from their wandering path
    Drags them by necessity, and they, being forced,
Follow not unwillingly; yet each completes its own journey,
    Backward, slower or faster.
By which, the circular love, lifting us from the earth on high,
    Burns us with the longing for heavenly beauty.
By which, you preserve the incorruptible nature of the soul, nor do you allow it
    To be dimmed, struck by the shadows of a perishing world.
At other times, you draft a city bordering the heavens for men,
    For whom noble Justice is a concern,
And Law, the nurse of youth; and from that city,
    They did not turn away; and so too again,
Reverence and Retribution; who could recount each thing
    That you placed in these god-inspired pages?
Having taken them, may you arrive at the queen of all cities,
    As many as the sun beholds from heaven,
The seven-hilled Rome, ever holding power over the earth.
    Through whose middle the Tiber, winding,
Goes as lord of the western rivers, horned,
    Fattening the udder of the Ausonian soil.
Having come, not to the malicious tyrant of the Sicilians there,
    The fosterling of the raw-eating, wretched Scylla,
The insolent Dionysius, who hated the Muses, but rather, to the divine man,
    Him whom you vainly longed to see as a man.
Both a leader of wisdom and a shepherd of the people,
    As many as inhabit all of Europe.
Laurean, the star of your beloved Florentine homeland,
    Bright one. But also of the most famous Medici,
A flourishing, beautiful shoot, glorious and fruit-bearing,
    Once John, but now a lion  managing countless
Lands, the most powerful key-holder of Olympus,
    Whom we now revere as we do Zeus.
Whom every king respects, kneeling, nor does any
    Of the scepter-bearers dare to contend against him.
Having entered the divinely-blessed palace, immediately, Plato,
    You will see many lovers in the halls,
Occupied with education and virtues; and pleasant conversationalists,
    And the living sages of the earth.

title: Omnia Platonis Opera (Aldine Editio Princeps)
author: Plato
greek:
τε καὶ τὰ λόγους, οὔτε κατὰ σημείων πομπὰς, οὔθ' ὕπαρ οὐδ' ὄναρ. οὕτως ἔφη ἐμοί γε καὶ αὐτῷ φαίνεται σοῦ λέγοντος. συγχωρεῖς ἄρα ἔφην τοῦτον τύπον δεύτερον εἶναι, ὡς ᾧ δεῖ περὶ θεῶν καὶ λέγειν καὶ ποιεῖν, ὡς μήτε αὐτοὺς γόητας ὄντας μεταβάλλειν ἑαυτοὺς, μήτε ἡμᾶς ψεύδεσι παράγειν ἐν λόγῳ ἢ ἔργῳ; συγχωρῶ. πολλὰ ἄρα ὁμήρου ἐπαινοῦντες ἄλλα, τοῦτο οὐκ ἐπαινεσόμεθα, τὴν τοῦ ἐνυπνίου πομπὴν ὑπὸ διὸς τῷ ἀγαμέμνονι. οὐδ' αἰσχύλου, ὅταν φῇ ἡ θέτις τὸν ἀπόλλω ἐν τοῖς αὑτῆς γάμοις ᾄδοντα,

> ἐνδατεῖσθαι τὰς ἑὰς εὐπαιδίας.
> νόσων τ' ἀπείρους, καὶ μακραίωνας βίους.
> ξύμπαντά τ' εἰπὼν θεοφιλὰς ἐμὰς τύχας,
> παιῶν' ἐπευφήμησεν, εὐθυμῶν ἐμέ.
> κἀγὼ δ' ἐφοίβου θεῖον ἀψευδὲς στόμα
> ἤλπιζον εἶναι, μαντικῇ βρύον τέχνῃ.
> ὁ δ' αὐτὸς ὑμνῶν, αὐτὸς ἐν θοίνῃ παρών.
> αὐτός τάδ' εἰπὼν, αὐτός ἐστιν ὁ κτανὼν
> τὸν παῖδα τὸν ἐμόν.

ὅταν τις τοιαῦτα λέγῃ περὶ θεῶν, χαλεπανοῦμέν τε, καὶ χορὸν οὐ δώσομεν, οὐδὲ τοὺς διδασκάλους ἐάσομεν ἐπὶ παιδείᾳ χρῆσθαι τῶν νέων. εἰ μέλλουσιν ἡμῖν οἱ φύλακες, θεοσεβεῖς τε καὶ θεῖοι γίγνεσθαι, καθ' ὅσον ἀνθρώπῳ ἐπὶ πλεῖστον οἷόν τε. παντάπασιν ἔφη ἔγωγε τοὺς τύπους τούτους συγχωρῶ, καὶ ὡς νόμοις ἂν χρώμην.

τέλος τοῦ πολιτειῶν ἢ περὶ δικαίου. β.

ΠΛΑΤΩΝΟΣ ΠΟΛΙΤΕΙΩΝ, Η ΠΕΡΙ ΔΙΚΑΙΟΥ ΤΡΙΤΟΣ.

Τὰ μὲν δὴ περὶ θεοὺς ὡς ἔοικε, τοιαῦτ' ἄττα ὡς ἔοικεν ἀκουστέον τε καὶ οὐκ ἀκουστέον, εὐθὺς ἐκ παίδων τοῖς θεούς τε τιμήσουσι, καὶ γονέας. τήν τε ἀλλήλων φιλίαν, μὴ περὶ σμικροῦ ποιησομένοις. καὶ οἶμαί γ' ἔφη ὀρθῶς ἡμῖν φαίνεσθαι. τί δὲ δὴ εἰ μέλλουσιν εἶναι ἀνδρεῖοι; ἆρ' οὐ ταῦτά τε λεκτέον, καὶ οἷα αὐτοὺς ποιήσει ἥκιστα τὸν θάνατον δεδιέναι, ἢ ἡγῇ τινά ποτ' ἂν γενέσθαι ἀνδρεῖον, ἔχοντα ἐν αὑτῷ τοῦτο τὸ δεῖμα; μὰ Δία ἦ δ' ὃς οὐκ ἔγωγε. τί δὲ τὰ ἐν ᾅδου ἡγούμενον εἶναί τε, καὶ δεινὰ εἶναι, οἴει τινὰ θανάτου ἀδεῆ ἔσεσθαι. καὶ ἐν ταῖς μάχαις αἱρήσεσθαι πρὸ ἥττης τε καὶ δουλείας θάνατον; οὐδαμῶς. δεῖ δὴ ὡς ἔοικεν ἡμᾶς ἐπιστατεῖν καὶ περὶ τούτων τῶν μύθων, τοῖς ἐπιχειροῦσι λέγειν. καὶ δεῖσθαι μὴ λοιδορεῖν ἁπλῶς οὕτω τὰ ἐν ᾅδου, ἀλλὰ μᾶλλον ἐπαινεῖν. ὡς οὔτ' ἀληθῆ λέγοντας, οὔτ' ὠφέλιμα τοῖς μέλλουσι μαχίμοις ἔσεσθαι. δεῖ μέντοι ἔφη. ἐξαλείψομεν ἄρα ὡς δ' ἐγὼ ἀπὸ τοῦδε τοῦ ἔπους ἀρξάμενοι πάντα τὰ τοιαῦτα.

> βουλοίμην κ' ἐπάρουρος ἐὼν θητευέμεν ἄλλῳ.
> ἀνδρὶ παρ' ἀκλήρῳ, ᾧ μὴ βίοτος πολὺς εἴη.
> ἢ πᾶσι νεκύεσσι καταφθιμένοισιν ἀνάσσειν. καὶ τό,
> οἰκία δὲ θνητοῖσι καὶ ἀθανάτοισι φανείη
> σμερδαλέ' εὐρώεντα, τά τε στυγέουσι θεοί περ. καὶ,
> ὢ πόποι, ἦ ῥά τις ἔστι καὶ εἰν ἀΐδαο δόμοισι
> ψυχὴ καὶ εἴδωλον, ἀτὰρ φρένες οὐκ ἔνι πάμπαν. καὶ τό,
> οἴῳ πεπνῦσθαι τοὶ δὲ σκιαὶ ἀΐσσουσιν. καὶ,
> ψυχὴ δ' ἐκ ῥεθέων πταμένη ἄϊδός δε βεβήκει.
english:
...or through stories, or through the sending of signs, neither when awake nor in a dream. In this way, I also think it appears to me, as you say. You grant, then, I said, that this second pattern is one which must be used when speaking and acting concerning the gods: that they are neither sorcerers themselves, changing their own form, nor do they lead us astray through lies in speech or deed? I grant it. Therefore, while we praise many other things of Homer, we shall not praise this: the sending of the dream by Zeus to Agamemnon. Nor Aeschylus, when he says that Thetis claimed Apollo sang at her wedding,

> "Recounting the good fortune of my offspring,
> And lives free from disease and long-lasting;
> And having spoken of all my fates as beloved by the gods,
> He sang a paean, cheering my heart.
> And I, for my part, hoped that Phoebus’ divine and truthful mouth
> Was brimming with the prophetic art.
> But he, the very one singing, the very one present at the feast,
> The very one saying these things, is the very one who slew
> My son."

When anyone says such things about the gods, we shall be angered, and we shall not grant them a chorus, nor shall we allow the teachers to use such things for the education of the young, if our guardians are to become god-fearing and god-like, in so far as it is possible for a human being. I entirely agree, he said, and I would use these patterns as laws.

End of the Republic or On Justice, II.

PLATO'S REPUBLIC, OR ON JUSTICE, THE THIRD.

The things concerning the gods, then, as it seems, are such things as one must and must not hear, beginning from childhood, for those who are to honor the gods and their parents, and not to consider their friendship for one another as a small thing. And I think, he said, that this appears correct to us. But what, then, if they are to be brave? Must not these things be said, and such things as will make them least of all fear death? Or do you suppose that anyone would ever become brave, having this terror within him? By Zeus, he said, I do not. But what, if he believes that the things in Hades exist and are terrible, do you think anyone will be fearless of death, and in battles will choose death over defeat and slavery? Not at all. It is necessary, then, as it seems, that we also oversee those who undertake to tell these myths, and request them not to disparage the things in Hades so simply, but rather to praise them, as they speak neither what is true nor what is useful for those who are to be warlike. It is necessary, indeed, he said. We shall therefore strike out, I said, starting from this verse, all such things:

> "I would rather be a serf, tied to the soil, serving another,
> A man without a portion, whose living is not great,
> Than rule over all the departed dead."

And this,

> "And the house, to mortals and to immortals, might appear
> Terrible and dank, which even the gods loathe."

And,

> "Alas, there is indeed, even in the house of Hades,
> A soul and an image, but there is no mind at all within."

And this,

> "The only one to be wise; the others flit as shadows."

And,

> "His soul, having flown from his limbs, went to Hades."

greek:
Ἆρ’ οὖν, ἔφην ἐγώ, ἄξιον ὅτι δεῖ αὐτοὺς τῆς ὀρθῆς τυχεῖν παιδείας, ἥ τις ποτέ ἐστιν, εἰ μέλλουσι τὸ μέγιστον ἔχειν, πρὸς τὸ ἥμεροι εἶναι αὐτοῖς τε, καὶ τοῖς φυλαττομένοις ὑπ’ αὐτῶν. Καὶ ὀρθῶς γε, ἦ δ’ ὅς. Πρὸς τοίνυν τῇ παιδείᾳ ταύτῃ, φαίη ἄν τις νοῦν ἔχων, δεῖν καὶ τὰς οἰκήσεις καὶ τὴν ἄλλην οὐσίαν, τοιαύτην αὐτοῖς παρεσκευάσθαι, ἥ τις μήτε τοὺς φύλακας ὡς ἀρίστους εἶναι παύσοι αὐτοὺς, κακουργεῖν τε μὴ ἐπάροι περὶ τοὺς ἄλλους πολίτας. Καὶ ἀληθῶς γε φήσει. Ὅρα δὴ εἶπον ἐγώ, εἰ τοιόνδε τινὰ τρόπον δεῖ αὐτοὺς ζῆν τε καὶ οἰκεῖν, εἰ μέλλουσι τοιοῦτοι ἔσεσθαι. πρῶτον μὲν οὐσίαν κεκτημένον μηδεμίαν μηδένα ἰδίαν, ἂν μὴ πᾶσα ἀνάγκη· ἔπειτα οἴκησιν καὶ ταμιεῖον μηδενὶ εἶναι μηδὲν τοιοῦτον, εἰς ὃ οὐ πᾶς ὁ βουλόμενος εἴσεισι. τὰ δ’ ἐπιτήδεια, ὅσων δέονται ἄνδρες ἀθληταὶ πολέμου σώφρονές τε καὶ ἀνδρεῖοι, ταξαμένους παρὰ τῶν ἄλλων πολιτῶν, δέχεσθαι μισθὸν τῆς φυλακῆς τοσοῦτον, ὅσον μήτε περιεῖναι αὐτοῖς εἰς τὸν ἐνιαυτὸν, μήτε ἐνδεῖν· φοιτῶντας δὲ εἰς ξυσσίτια ὡς παρ’ ἐστρατοπεδευμένους, κοινῇ ζῆν. χρυσίον δὲ καὶ ἀργύριον εἰπεῖν αὐτοῖς, ὅτι θεῖον παρὰ θεῶν αἰεὶ ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ ἔχουσι, καὶ οὐδὲν προσδέονται τοῦ ἀνθρωπείου. οὐδὲ ὅσια τὴν ἐκείνου κτῆσιν, τῇ τοῦ θνητοῦ χρυσοῦ κτήσει, ξυμμιγνύντας, μιαίνειν· διότι πολλὰ καὶ ἀνόσια, περὶ τὸ τῶν πολλῶν νόμισμα γέγονε· τὸ παρ’ ἐκείνοις δὲ ἀκήρατον. ἀλλὰ μόνοις αὐτοῖς τῶν ἐν τῇ πόλει μεταχειρίζεσθαι καὶ ἅπτεσθαι χρυσοῦ καὶ ἀργύρου, οὐ θέμις, οὐδ’ ὑπὸ τὸν αὐτὸν ὄροφον ἰέναι· οὐδὲ περιαψάσθαι, οὐδὲ πίνειν ἐξ ἀργύρου ἢ χρυσοῦ, καὶ οὕτω μὲν σώζειν τ’ ἂν καὶ σώζειν τὴν πόλιν· ὁπότε δ’ αὐτοὶ, γῆν τε ἰδίαν καὶ οἰκίας καὶ νομίσματα κτήσονται, οἰκονόμοι μὲν καὶ γεωργοὶ, ἀντὶ φυλάκων ἔσονται. δεσπόται δ’ ἐχθροὶ, ἀντὶ συμμάχων τῶν ἄλλων πολιτῶν γενήσονται. μισοῦντες δὲ δὴ καὶ μισούμενοι καὶ ἐπιβουλεύοντες, καὶ ἐπιβουλευόμενοι, διάξουσι πάντα τὸν βίον, πολὺ πλείω καὶ μᾶλλον δεδιότες τοὺς ἔνδον, ἢ τοὺς ἔξωθεν πολεμίους. θέοντες ἤδη τότε ἐγγύτατα ὀλέθρου, αὐτοί τε, καὶ ἡ ἄλλη πόλις. τούτων οὖν, πάντων ἕνεκα, μὴ οὕτω φῶμεν οὕτω δεῖν κατεσκευάσθαι τοὺς φύλακας, οἰκήσεώς τε πέρι καὶ τῶν ἄλλων.

"Is it then," I said, "a thing of importance that they should attain the correct education, whatever it may be, if they are to have the greatest advantage for being gentle both to themselves and to those who are guarded by them?"
"And rightly so," he said.
"With respect, therefore, to this education, any sensible person would say that their dwellings and their other property must be so prepared that they neither prevent the guardians from being the best they can be, nor incite them to do evil to the other citizens."
"And he will say so with truth," he replied.
"Consider then," I said, "if it is in some such way as this that they ought to live and dwell, if they are to be such as we describe. First, that no one should possess any private property at all, unless there is absolute necessity. Next, that no one should have any dwelling or storeroom into which anyone who wishes may not enter. As for their necessities, such as are required by temperate and brave athletes of war, they should receive from the other citizens as a salary for their guardianship, such an amount as would neither leave them with a surplus at the end of the year, nor leave them in want. They must attend common messes as if they were in a camp, and live in common. We must tell them that they possess a divine gold and silver from the gods, always within their souls, and have no need of the human sort; nor is it holy to contaminate the possession of that divine metal by mingling it with the possession of mortal gold, because many unholy things have been done for the sake of the currency of the masses, whereas that which they possess is pure. Indeed, for them alone of all in the city, it is not permitted to handle or touch gold and silver, nor to come under the same roof, nor to wear it as an ornament, nor to drink from silver or gold. In this way, they would save themselves and save the city. But whenever they acquire private land, houses, and currency, they will be housekeepers and farmers instead of guardians; they will become hostile masters instead of allies to the other citizens; hating and being hated, plotting and being plotted against, they will pass their entire lives fearing the enemies within much more than those without; and they, along with the rest of the city, will then be rushing toward the very brink of destruction. For the sake of all these things, let us say that the guardians must not be established in such a way, both regarding their housing and other matters."

PLATO'S LAWS OR ON LEGISLATION
Plato's laws or on legislation

GOD Theos, or some human being, has provided you with the cause for the arrangement of your laws, strangers? It is a god, stranger, it is a god, as it is most just to say. Among us it is Zeus king of the Olympian gods, and among the Lacedaemonians Spartans, from where this man comes, I believe one would say it is Apollo god of prophecy and music. Is that not so? Yes. Are you speaking in accordance with Homer ancient Greek epic poet, that Minos legendary king of Crete used to visit his father every nine years, and through the rumors and teachings from him, he established the laws for your cities? It is indeed said so among us, and certainly his brother Rhadamanthus—for the name is well-known—is said to have been the most just of men. We Cretans would say he received that praise because, at that time, he judged legal matters correctly. It was a noble pursuit, and quite fitting for a son of Zeus. Since we have been brought up under such laws, I expect that it will not be unpleasant for us to speak about government and laws while we walk. In any case, the road from Knossos ancient city on Crete to the cave and sanctuary of Zeus is long enough, and there are likely shaded places along the way among the tall trees, especially as it is quite hot now. It would be appropriate for men of our age to rest frequently in them, and to converse with one another.

I may also answer what you ask: how I and you ought to be toward one another. If you have altogether looked down on philosophy, let it go. But if you have heard better things from another or have found better yourself than those from me, honor those. If, however, the things from us please you, then I also should be honored most. Now then, just as in the beginning, you lead and I will follow. For being honored by you, I will honor you, but not being honored, I will keep silent. Moreover, if you honor me and lead in this, you will seem to honor philosophy, and this very fact, that you examined others also, will bring you a good reputation among many as being a philosopher. But if I honor you when you do not honor me, I will seem to admire and pursue wealth, and we know that this name is not good among all men. To speak in sum: if you honor me, it is a credit to both, but if I honor you without return, it is a reproach to both. So much then for these matters.

...that this is not a single matter, nor is it infinite in its own right. But if indeed they establish the rare and the dense as the primary principles, as some authorities claim; for those who make the dense and the rare their principles, the underlying matter is effectively the same as the "dense." Likewise, the "rare" also serves as matter for it. For neither is Love  a part of the form, nor is their Strife ; nor is Strife separated from the matter itself, but rather these opposites exist within it.

To me, it seems they also treat the "forms" as what they call the "nature of the elements"—a topic regarding which we have already raised some general difficulties. Even if the nature of Love is part of their hypothesis, we do not assume the opposites of these same natures. It is entirely clear that some do not even speak of the principle as existing by itself. There is, however, a principle of the divine substance, and the individual thing seems to be a principle and prior in existence. And the essence found within being is also distinct; yet these terms do not signify the same thing. Or rather, they assume every essence to be prior; wherefore, concerning the former ... so as to be a definition.

And among these, whatever cause they preserve within both of them the whole, or what the entire thing becomes; just as we might suppose the entire form to be agreeable. But whatever it is, or the intermediate state between them, it seems to be the same... for fire, air, water, and earth are woven together from these. It is for this reason we do not call such a thing "the subject," which they make in relation to another ... for it is indeed essence, either according to the differences or the causes of other things. It would possess the whole, but everything would be its opposite. They live in a certain shape ... such as by density and rarity, ... greater and lesser. These things you would preserve entirely as outright riddles, just as the other is contained. And yet, there are many things, and the common opinion is that nothing exists.

...indeed the gods as well. Is he then your enemy? But so that I do not appear too hostile to you, and whatever measure seems right to you, they differ about this very thing. And look at it according to the same reasoning: tell me, by Zeus, have you ever seen another one of the gods killing your father?  Because of me, do you think the holy hosion: that which is sanctioned by divine law or "pious" would cease to be if some human child, Euthyphro—let us not say what!—But the gods surely do disagree, as I was saying. Some say one thing, others say another.

They do not give in on my account, nor do they cease disputing these things, both gods and men. Or does someone say otherwise? But I must try to say what you perhaps do not: what? Is it not about honor? Or do they agree, O Euthyphro? Regarding wrongdoers, though they agree, they still deny that they themselves are doing wrong. Not at all, then; nothing strange will they show or say. I think they would much rather dispute immediately that they are not the ones doing wrong.

What about the father? Both say they are not doing wrong, or do they? You speak the truth. Therefore, they do not dispute with the gods that the wrongdoer must pay the penalty dikên didonai: literally "to give justice," meaning to undergo punishment. But what? I think they argue whether those who did these things spoke the truth, or as the gods say, or whether they will not kill. For he does not dare to do wrong to you or to the holy, this man. And some say... it is true for me. They said they knew. It is a wonder to me, my friend, for no one of gods or men dares to say that one who does wrong should not pay the penalty. By the gods, you speak the truth, Socrates.

But the main point: I think I have grown weary, O Euthyphro, of the arguments of those who dispute—both men and gods—if indeed the gods dispute as you say. Regarding the things you differ on: some say you have acted justly, others unjustly. Could someone hold this? Certainly. Come then, my dear Euthyphro, teach me as well, so that I may become wiser. οἱ βάρβιοι δὲ πονηρὰ πικρὸν τὸν μάγον τὸν δυσπύρου,
ξύλινα λεία πρόσωπα σάρδεσιν ἐπικλίσαι.
ἐν ὕπαιθρ’ μήκεσι γὰρ τοῖς, νύκτωρ ἐνδεδυμή.

πρὸς ἀστυάγην πατέρα μητρὸς ὁ κῦρος πεποίηκαν.

english:
For he was the general of Phrygia and the Hellespont,
And Arrybocus was king of all Cappadocia.
And another multitude of countless, varied nations,
And with them was the king of the Mysians, Arrybas.
And this Croesus the Lydian, who is the subject of the words.
So when Cyrus joined battle with them,
He marched upon Sardis. On the second night,
The Chaldeans caused them to ascend the walls and the gates.

The founder, this Astyages, son of Astyochus,
Departed from the city out of the danger of the bitterness.
And Artaxerxes, having been captured as an ally of the Persians,
Remained among the Persians for seventeen years.
For books and writers also record these things.
They say that Astyages, having been captured by Cyrus,
Was handed over to be ruled by some of the Hyrcanians.
The barbarians, the evil and bitter magicians of the fire-temple,
Made wooden faces to incline toward Sardis.
For at night, they were clothed in those empty lengths.
Thus the Lydians were troubled and lost the city.
After the capture of Croesus, they say,
Cyrus moved against Astyages, his mother's father,
So that by coming to the springs of his own people with them,
And the child of Astyages not being alive,
He made the first death a miserable one.

I.

TO APOLLO.

I will remember and not be unmindful of Apollo who shoots from afar,
whom the gods tremble at as he enters the house of Zeus.
They all spring up from their seats as he approaches,
whenever he stretches his bright bow.
Only Leto remains beside Zeus who delights in thunder, 5
until she unstrings his bow and closes his quiver.
Then, taking the bow from his strong shoulders with her hands,
she hangs it against a pillar of his father's house,
from a golden peg, and leads him to a throne to sit.
To him the father gives nectar in a golden cup, 10
welcoming his dear son, and then the other deities sit.
Then they sit down; and lady Leto  rejoices,
because she bore a bow-bearing and powerful son.
[Hail, blessed Leto, since you bore glorious children,

her in Ortygia and him in rocky Delos,
as you leaned against the great mountain and the Cynthian hill,
very near the palm tree, by the streams of Inopus.]
How then shall I sing of you, you who are in every way well-worthy of song?

english:
1. TO APOLLO.

...to bring Eileithyia, promising her a great necklace,
strung with gold and amber, nine cubits long.
 They told her to call her away from the sight of white-armed Hera,
lest Hera later turn her back with words as she set out.
When Iris, whose feet are swift as the wind, heard this,
she began to run, and she quickly crossed all the distance between.
 When she reached the home of the gods, steep Olympus,
she immediately called Eileithyia out from the hall to the door.
She spoke winged words to her,
telling her everything exactly as the goddesses who live on Olympus had commanded.
She persuaded the heart within her breast.
 They went forth with steps like timid doves.

When Eileithyia, who helps in labor, set foot on Delos,
the birth pangs took hold of Leto, and she longed to give birth.
She threw her arms around a palm tree and braced her knees
on the soft meadow. The earth smiled beneath her.
 The child leapt forth into the light. All the goddesses cried out in joy.
There, O lord Phoebus, the goddesses washed you in beautiful water,
holily and purely. They wrapped you in a white cloth,
fine and newly made, and they placed a golden band around you.
Apollo of the golden sword was not nursed by his mother.
Instead, Themis gave him nectar and lovely ambrosia
 with her immortal hands. Leto was glad
because she had given birth to a strong son who carries a bow.
But when you had eaten the divine food, Phoebus,
the golden bands could no longer hold you as you struggled.
The cords did not restrain you, and all your bonds were loosened.
 Immediately Phoebus Apollo spoke among the goddesses:
"May the lyre and the curved bow be dear to me,
and I will reveal to men the unerring will of Zeus."

OF HOMER’S ILIAD
The First Rhapsody.

Alpha: The prayers, the gold, the plague, the army, the anger of the lords.

 Sing, Goddess, the anger of Achilles, son of Peleus,
destructive, which brought countless pains to the Achaeans, gave to them
and sent many mighty souls of heroes to Hades,
and made them prey for dogs
and all birds;
and the will of Zeus was being fulfilled;
from the time when the first two stood apart, having quarreled,
the son of Atreus, king of men, and godlike Achilles.
Who then of the gods set them to fight in strife?
The son of Leto and Zeus; for he, having been angered at the king,
roused an evil disease through the army, and the people were perishing,
because the son of Atreus dishonored the priest Chryses.
For he came to the swift ships of the Achaeans
to ransom his daughter, and bringing boundless ransom,
having in his hands the fillets of far-shooting Apollo
on a golden staff, and he was entreating all the Achaeans,
but especially the two sons of Atreus, the marshals of the people:
"Sons of Atreus, and other well-greaved Achaeans,
may the gods who possess Olympian homes grant you..."

who might say why Phoebus Apollo is so angered;

"O Achilles, you order me, beloved of Zeus, to speak

Therefore I will speak; but do you swear and pledge to me

english:
Of Homer's Iliad.
Book I.
Summary of the Rhapsody.

Chryses, priest of Apollo, arrives at the naval camp of the Greeks, wishing to redeem his daughter Chryseis. Having not received her, but rather being driven away with insults by Agamemnon, he prayed to Apollo against the Greeks. A plague having occurred and many, as is to be expected, perishing, Achilles gathered an assembly. Calchas having clarified the true cause, and having ordered Achilles to appease the god, Agamemnon, angered, disputed with Achilles and snatched away his prize, Briseis. He then becomes angry with the Greeks. Thetis, having been implored by her son, went up to Olympus and requested of Zeus that he make the Trojans stronger than the Greeks. Hera, knowing this, disputed with Zeus until Hephaestus reconciled them by pouring wine into a golden cup. The rest of the day, having feasted, they turn to sleep.

Alexander the Great, Monarch of the world, was accustomed to name the Homeric Iliad as a military instruction. And he loved the volume itself to such a degree that he would sleep with it together with his dagger under his pillow, saying he preferred to excel in these things rather than in riches.

...took for you, when you made plans for me in my wretchedness
...of the war, for you are keeping near...
But he kissed... light from... dear clothes, the two
The cloak and the tunic; for they cover you thus...
But he himself, weeping, they ran under the ships...
Having struck from the assembly with disgraceful blows.
So he spoke, and with the scepter upon his back and shoulders
He struck him; and he doubled up, and a thick tear fell from him.
And a bloody weal rose up on his back
From under the golden scepter; and he sat down and trembled
Having suffered pain, and looking helpless, he wiped away his tear.
And they, though grieving, laughed pleasantly at him;
And thus someone would say, looking to the one near him:
O gods, truly Odysseus has done ten thousand good things,
Leading good councils, and preparing for war;
But now this is the greatest good he has done among the Argives;
He who kept the reviler, the abusive one, from the assemblies;
His high-minded spirit will not again incite him
To rail at kings with insulting words.
So said the multitude; and up stood the sacker of cities, Odysseus
Holding the scepter; and beside him bright-eyed Athena
Appearing as a herald, ordered the people to be silent;
So that at the same time the first and the last sons of the Achaeans
Might hear the speech and ponder the council.
He, being well-minded, spoke to them and addressed them:
Son of Atreus, now indeed the Achaeans want
To make you the most disgraceful among all mortal men;
Nor do they fulfill the promise which they undertook
When still walking here from horse-pasturing Argos
To return home after sacking well-walled Ilium.

CONCERNING HOMER AND
HESIOD, AND THE
story of their contest.

All people desire to claim Homer and Hesiod, the most divine poets, as their own citizens. But Hesiod, by naming his own homeland, relieved everyone of this contention by saying that his father,

> Settled near Helicon, in a miserable village,
> Ascra, bad in winter, hard in summer, and never good.

Homer, however, is claimed by almost all cities and their colonies to have been born among them. The Smyrnians are the first to say that he was the son of Meles, the river among them, and the nymph Critheis, and that he was previously called Melesigenes; yet later, having been blinded, he was renamed Homer, on account of the term habitual among them for such people. The Chians, in turn, bring forward evidence that he is their own citizen, saying that some of his descendants still survive among them, who are called the Homeridae. The Colophonians even point out the place where they say he began his poetry while teaching letters, and composed the Margites first.

> The bronze light, from the shining helmets,
> And newly polished breastplates, and glittering shields,
> Coming together; very bold-hearted would he be
> Who would rejoice then, seeing the labor, and not grieve.

The Greeks, having marveled at Homer even in this, praised him as if the verses were spoken appropriately; and they ordered that the victory be given to him. But the king crowned Hesiod, saying that it was just that one who calls people to agriculture and peace should win, not one who recounts wars and slaughters. They say that Hesiod attained the victory in this way; and having taken a bronze tripod, he dedicated it to the Muses, having inscribed upon it,

> Hesiod dedicated this to the Heliconian Muses,
> Having won in Chalcis with his hymn against divine Homer.

When the contest was dissolved, Hesiod sailed across to Delphi to consult the oracle, and to dedicate the first fruits of his victory to the god. As he approached the temple, they say that the prophetess, becoming inspired, said,

> Blessed is this man who walks about my house,
> Hesiod, honored by the immortal Muses;
> His fame shall be as great as the dawn spreads.
> But guard yourself against the beautiful grove of Nemean Zeus;
> There is the fated end of your death.

Hesiod, having heard the oracle, withdrew from the Peloponnese, thinking that the god was speaking of the Nemea there; and he went to Oinoe in Locris.

THE ACCOUNT OF HERODOTUS OF HALICARNASSUS
REGARDING THE ORIGIN
OF HOMER
AND HIS LIFE

Herodotus of Halicarnassus has recorded these things concerning the origin, age, and life of Homer, having sought to investigate them with the greatest accuracy. When ancient Aeolian Cyme was being founded, various Greek tribes came together in one place, including those from Magnesia and others, and among them was Melanopus, a native of Crithon, who was not wealthy but lived in modest circumstances. This Melanopus married the daughter of Homer in Cyme, and she bore him a female child, who was named Critheïs. Melanopus himself eventually died. The daughter was then entrusted to a man whom she used to associate with frequently, Cleonax the Argive. As time passed, it happened that the girl, having secretly lain with a man, conceived. At first, it remained hidden, but when Cleonax noticed, he was distressed by the circumstance. Calling Critheïs aside, he held her in great reproach, anticipating the shame it would bring among the citizens. He deliberated regarding her as follows: It happened that the people of Cyme were building the Hermean Gulf; while they were building the city, they named it Smyrna, desiring to establish a memorial named after his own wife, for her name was Smyrna. PAOLO MANUZIO, SON OF ALDO, to the most reverend father, Ludovico Beccadelli, Bishop of Ragusa and Legate to the Archbishop of Venice, greetings.

I believe everyone knows what my father contributed to this art of printing. For he took it when it was still quite impoverished and neglected, and he was so ambitious that he expanded and transformed it, so that he left nothing of value to his successors in this field. I have long desired to follow in my father's undertakings, not desiring to prove myself inferior to him, but I have been weighed down by all kinds of busyness and the writings I have in hand. Moreover, not having a wealth of money, I preferred to remain quiet and leave things as they were, rather than to attempt what was beyond my strength and not achieve the value I expected. Yet many of my friends, who seemed to be well-disposed toward me, would daily attempt to rebuke me, saying that it was shameful if, having the greatest and finest resources regarding my father, I should willingly do evil out of laziness, and allow myself to be marginalized by those whom I should least allow, and allow fate to be corrupted by the greed of others, while I could instead follow in his footsteps and prepare for myself an everlasting monument for future time. These people, then, who seemed to have good intentions, did not escape my notice.

OLYNTHUS is a city of Thrace, but the
people inhabiting it are of the
Greek race from Chalcis in Euboea.
Chalcis is a colony of the Athenians. There
were many and famous wars of Olynthus.
For it fought against the Athenians
ruling the Greeks in ancient times,
and again against the Lacedaemonians. In time it attained
to great power, and held sway over the related cities.
For the Chalcidian race is great in Thrace. The Olynthians,
having made an alliance with Philip, the king of the
Macedonians, and fighting together with him against the
Athenians at the beginning, both because of those things
that they took before the Macedonian, a city disputed by the
Macedonians and Olynthians, and because of Potidaea, which,
having besieged while the Athenians held it, Philip gave
to the Olynthians; later, they began to fear the king,
seeing his rapid and great growth, and not trusting his
intention. Having kept him under observation, they sent
ambassadors to the Athenians and dissolved the war against
them, having made [a pact] according to the treaties with
Philip. For they had agreed to fight the Athenians in
common, and if anything else should seem [right], to decide
in common. But Philip, having long desired them, then
taking this as a violation of the treaties, and because they
had sought friendship with his enemies, brought war against
them. They sent ambassadors to the Athenians for aid, to
whom Demosthenes speaks in support, urging them to aid
the Olynthians.

english:
MARCUS MUSURUS
TO JANUS LASCARIS,
HEARTY GREETINGS.

I have often marveled at those who are ill-disposed toward our present circumstances, but are accustomed to praising only the most ancient things, and who complain that Nature was a fond mother to the ancients, but is to us a spiteful stepmother. For they claim that every science and art flourished of old and reached the highest state of perfection, but now withers away and, through neglect, flows down into a worse condition. Now, one might refute such people for unjustly accusing this age of ours on other grounds—for many and wonderful things have been discovered in our time, the conception of which antiquity seems not even to have imagined in a dream—and particularly by the construction of engines of war. For truly, the many-tiered helepoles and the ram-bearing tortoises would be considered but childish toys compared to the stone-throwing basilisks, by which we, when besieging walls, could take by force even the heaven-reaching pyramids of the Egyptians and the asphalt-bound battlements of Semiramis, and easily consume them together with the thunderous and all-consuming discharge of a three-talent cylinder, shattering like a thunderbolt falling from above everything that offers resistance. Yet the ingenuity of these military instruments is not so much a testament to the resourcefulness of men born in recent times as it has proved ruinous to those who excel in manliness and experience of war. For "the excellence of man is perished," and "it has loosed the heads of many cities, and yet shall loose them"; looking upon these things, one might reasonably groan. But as for the innovation of types, through which, from a single manuscript as if from some most fertile trunk, myriad offshoots of books are born, being both beneficial to life and the cause of great blessings—for what greater or more gentle benefit could the gods provide to the race of men...

greek: Ἐξ ἀρχῆς χῶμα γῆς, ὕστερον δὲ τοῦ θεοῦ χρήσαντος, ἐκοσμήθη λίθῳ κογχίτῃ. μόνοις δὲ Ἑλλήνων Μεγαρεῦσιν ὁ κογχίτης οὗτός ἐστι, καὶ σφίσι καὶ ἐν τῇ πόλει πεποίηται πολλὰ ἐξ αὐτοῦ. Ἔστι δὲ ἄγαν λευκὸς, καὶ ἄλλου λίθου μαλακώτερος· κόγχοι δὲ αἱ θαλάσσιαι διὰ παντὸς ἔνεισίν οἱ. Αὐτὸς μὲν τοιοῦτός ἐστιν ὁ λίθος. τὴν δὲ ὀνομαζομένην ἀπὸ Σκίρωνος καὶ ἐς τόδε Σκιρωνίαν, ἡνίκα Μεγαρεῦσιν ἐπολέμησε, πρῶτος, ὡς λέγουσιν, ἐποίησεν ἀνδράσιν εὐζώνοις ὁδεύειν. Ἀδριανὸς δὲ ὁ βασιλεὺς καὶ οὕτως, ὡς καὶ ἅρματα ἐναντία ἐλαύνεσθαι, κατέστησεν εὐρυχωρῆ τε καὶ ἐπιτηδείαν εἶναι. Λόγοι δέ εἰσιν ἐς τὰς πέτρας αἳ κατὰ τὸ στενὸν τῆς ὁδοῦ μάλιστα ἀνέχουσιν, ἐς μὲν τὴν Μολουρίδα, ὡς ἀπὸ ταύτης αὑτὴν ἐς θάλασσαν Ἰνὼ ῥίψαι, Μελικέρτην ἔχουσα τῶν παίδων νεώτερον· τὸν γὰρ δὴ πρεσβύτερον αὐτῶν Λέαρχον, ἀπέκτεινεν ὁ πατήρ. Λέγεται μὲν δὴ καὶ μανέντα δρᾶσαι ταῦτα Ἀθάμαντα· λέγεται δὲ καὶ ὡς εἰς τὴν Ἰνὼ καὶ τοὺς ἐξ αὐτῆς παῖδας χρήσαιτο ἀκρατεῖ τῷ θυμῷ, τὸν συμβάντα Ὀρχομενίοις λοιμὸν καὶ τὸν δοκοῦντα Φρίξου θάνατον αἰσθόμενος, οὗ θεῖον αἴτιον οὐδὲν, βουλεῦσαι δὲ ἐπὶ τούτοις πᾶσιν Ἰνὼ μητρυιὰν οὖσαν. Τότε δὲ φεύγουσα ἐς θάλασσαν, αὑτὴν καὶ τὸν παῖδα ἀπὸ τῆς πέτρας τῆς Μολουρίδος ἀφίησιν. Ἐξενεχθέντος δὲ ἐς τὸν Κορινθίων Ἰσθμὸν ὑπὸ δελφῖνος (ὡς λέγεται) τοῦ παιδὸς, τιμαὶ καὶ ἄλλαι τῷ Μελικέρτῃ δίδονται μετονομασθέντι Παλαίμονι, καὶ τῶν Ἰσθμίων ἐπ’ αὐτῷ τὸν ἀγῶνα ἄγουσι. Τὴν μὲν δὴ Μολουρίδα πέτραν Λευκοθέας καὶ Παλαίμονος ἱερὰν ἥγουντο· τὰς δὲ μετὰ ταύτην, νομίζουσιν ἐναγεῖς, ὅτι παροικῶν σφίσιν ὁ Σκίρων, ὁπόσοις τῶν ξένων ἐπετύγχανεν, ἠφίει σφᾶς ἐς τὴν θάλασσαν. χελώνη δὲ ὑπενήχετο ταῖς πέτραις, τοὺς ἐσβληθέντας ἁρπάζειν· εἰσὶ δὲ αἱ θαλάσσιαι, πλὴν μεγέθους καὶ ποδῶν, ὅμοιαι ταῖς χερσαίαις, πόδας δὲ ἐοικότας ἔχουσι ταῖς φώκαις. Τούτων περιῆλθεν ἡ δίκη Σκίρωνα ἀφεθέντα ἐς θάλασσαν τὴν αὐτὴν ὑπὸ Θησέως. Ἐπὶ δὲ τῷ ὄρει τῆς ἄκρᾳ, Διός ἐστιν Ἀφεσίου καλουμένου ναός. Φασὶ δὲ ἐπὶ τῷ συμβάντος ποτὲ τοῖς Ἕλλησιν αὐχμοῦ, θύσαντος Αἰακοῦ, κατά τι δὴ λόγιον, τῷ Πανελληνίῳ Διὶ ἐν Αἰγίνῃ, κομίσαντα δὲ ἀφεῖναι, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο Ἀφέσιον καλεῖσθαι τὸν Δία. Ἐνταῦθα καὶ Ἀφροδίτης ἄγαλμά καὶ Ἀπόλλωνός ἐστι καὶ Πανός. προελθοῦσι δὲ ἐς τὸ πρόσω, μνῆμά ἐστιν Εὐρυσθέως. φεύγοντα δὲ ἐκ τῆς Ἀττικῆς μετὰ τὴν πρὸς Ἡρακλείδας μάχην ἐνταῦθα ἀποθανεῖν αὐτὸν ὑπὸ Ἰολάου λέγουσιν. Ἐκ ταύτης τῆς ὁδοῦ καταβᾶσιν Ἀπόλλωνος ἱερόν ἐστι Λατῴου. Καὶ μετ’ αὐτὸ Μεγαρεῦσιν ὅροι πρὸς τὴν Κορινθίαν· ἔνθα Ὕλλον τὸν Ἡρακλέους μονομαχῆσαι πρὸς τὸν Ἀρκάδα Ἔχεμον λέγουσιν.

Originally it was a mound of earth, but later, after the god had given an oracle, it was adorned with mussel-stone. Among the Greeks, the Megarians alone possess this mussel-stone, and many things in their city have been made from it. It is very white and softer than other stone; sea-mussels are found throughout it. Such is the nature of the stone itself. As for the road called Scironian to this day after Sciron, it is said that he, when he was polemarch of the Megarians, first made it passable for active men. But the Emperor Hadrian made it wide and suitable even for chariots to be driven in opposite directions.

There are stories told concerning the rocks which rise up especially at the narrow part of the road; as for the Molurian rock, it is said that from it Ino threw herself into the sea, holding the younger of her sons, Melicertes—for their father had killed Learchus, the elder of them. It is said indeed that Athamas did these things in a fit of madness; but it is also said that he gave way to ungovernable rage against Ino and the children born of her, when he perceived that the famine which befell the Orchomenians and the supposed death of Phrixus had no divine cause, but that Ino, being their stepmother, had plotted all these things.

Then, fleeing to the sea, she cast herself and her son from the Molurian rock. When the child was carried to the Isthmus of the Corinthians by a dolphin (as they say), other honors were given to Melicertes, who was renamed Palaemon, and they celebrate the Isthmian games in his honor. The Molurian rock they held to be sacred to Leucothea and Palaemon; but the rocks after it they consider accursed, because Sciron, who dwelt near them, used to cast into the sea all the strangers he happened upon. A tortoise used to swim under the rocks to snatch up those who were thrown in; sea-tortoises are like land ones, except in size and feet, for their feet are like those of seals. For these deeds Sciron suffered punishment by being cast into the same sea by Theseus.

On the summit of the mountain is a temple of Zeus, called Aphesius. They say that on account of a drought which once befell the Greeks, when Aeacus had sacrificed to Zeus Panhellenius in Aegina according to an oracle, the rain was released, and for this reason Zeus is called Aphesius. Here also are statues of Aphrodite, Apollo, and Pan. As one proceeds further, there is the tomb of Eurystheus. They say that while fleeing from Attica after the battle against the Heraclidae, he died here at the hands of Iolaus. Going down from this road, there is a sanctuary of Apollo Latous. After this are the boundaries of the Megarians toward the Corinthian land, where they say that Hyllus, the son of Heracles, fought a duel with Echemus the Arcadian.

english:
THE ACHARNIANS

 A rope dripping with ruddle, used to sweep in loiterers from the Agora.

Like now, when the appointed Assembly is here
And it is morning, yet this Pnyx is empty;
They are talking in the Agora, and up and down
They flee from the rope stained with red ochre .
Even the prytaneis presiding magistrates have not arrived, but when they do,
They come at an ungodly hour, and then you cannot imagine how they shove
And scramble for the front bench,
Pouring in all at once. But as for how there might be peace,
They care for nothing; oh city, city!
I, however, am always the very first to come to the Assembly,
And I sit down; then, when I am alone,
I groan, I gape, I stretch, I fart,
I am at a loss, I write, I pluck my hair, I do my sums,
Looking away toward my farm, yearning for peace,
Loathing the town, and longing for my own village,
Which never said, "Buy charcoal,"
Or "vinegar," or "oil," and never even knew the word "buy,"
But itself provided everything, and the seller was absent.
So now I have come, thoroughly prepared
To shout, to heckle, to abuse the speakers,
If anyone talks of anything other than peace.
But here come the prytaneis presiding magistrates at noon.
Did I not say so? This is that very thing I was saying;
Every man is jostling for the front seat.

 CRIER. Come forward,
Come forward, so that you may be inside the consecrated boundary.

 AMPHITHEUS. Has anyone spoken yet?

 CRIER. Who wishes to speak?

 AMPHITHEUS. I.

CR. Who are you?

AM. Amphitheus.

CR. Not a man?

AM. No,
but immortal. For the first Amphitheus was of Demeter
and Triptolemus; from him comes Celeus;
Celeus married Phaenarete, my grandmother,
from whom Lycinus was born; from him I am
immortal; and the gods entrusted to me
alone the task of making a truce with the Lacedaemonians.
But though I am immortal, men, I have no travel money;
for the prytaneis presiding magistrates do not provide it.

CR. Archers!

AM. O Triptolemus and Celeus, will you look on while I am dragged away?

DI. Men of the prytaneis presiding magistrates, you wrong the Assembly
by dragging away the man who wanted to make a truce
for us and to hang up our shields.

CR. Sit down, silence!

DI. By Apollo, I will not,
unless you preside for me regarding the peace.

CR. The ambassadors from the Great King.

DI. Which King? I am sick of ambassadors
and their peacocks and their humbug.

CR. Silence!

DI. Good heavens, Ecbatana, what an outfit.

AMBASSADOR. You sent us to the Great King,
carrying a salary of two drachmas a day
when Euthymenes was archon chief magistrate.

+ For all other people who have desired to participate in philosophia love of wisdom/philosophy, they put matters to the test with demonstrations, and in this way, they bring conviction to their listeners. But the disciples of Christ confirmed the truth not through the persuasive words of human wisdom, but through the demonstration of the Spirit and power. For the work was not of men, but the accomplishment of God.

+ Furthermore, one must not be ignorant of this: that some know their arts and sciences of their own accord, but the prophets received their revelations from God. And some seek glory from men, and for this reason, they invent probabilities; but others look only to the glory of God. Indeed, some write at great length about spherical constructions, the oppositions of planets and stars, and such things, which contribute nothing to piety; but others, while they do not promise anything solemn, confirm the truth of things through teachings and instructions that are adapted to the soul and lead us toward God.

+ If, therefore, O man, you wish to learn precisely how you might obtain grace from God, listen to the dogmas of His piety. For these will lead you to the truth and to eternal life.
